questions.q: How is a deadlock different from ordinary blocking?
options: Ordinary blocking resolves itself when the holder commits or rolls back; a deadlock is a cycle where neither side can ever proceed on its own
A deadlock is just a longer version of ordinary blocking
Deadlocks only happen with SELECT statements, never with UPDATE
There is no real difference — they are the same thing
questions.explain: A deadlock specifically involves two or more transactions each waiting on a resource the other holds, with no path to resolution without intervention.

questions.q: In the classic two-resource deadlock example, what creates the cycle?
options: Session A holds a lock on Product 680 and wants Product 681, while Session B holds a lock on Product 681 and wants Product 680
Both sessions want to update the same single row at the same time
Session A and Session B are both read-only transactions
Session A's transaction never actually took any lock
questions.explain: Each session holds what the other wants, and each is waiting for the other to release first — that mutual wait is the cycle.

questions.q: What does SQL Server's deadlock monitor do when it detects a cycle?
options: It picks one transaction as the deadlock victim, kills it, and rolls it back so the other can proceed
It pauses the entire server until an administrator intervenes manually
It automatically merges both transactions into one
It silently ignores the cycle until the connection times out
questions.explain: The deadlock monitor is a background process that detects cycles and resolves them by rolling back the chosen victim, releasing its locks.

questions.q: What does error 1205 mean, and what is the application expected to do about it?
options: It means the session's transaction was chosen as the deadlock victim and rolled back, and it is expected to be retried
It means the database connection has been permanently closed
It means a syntax error occurred in the UPDATE statement
It means the table's schema was modified mid-query
questions.explain: Error 1205 is SQL Server reporting that this transaction was the deadlock victim; retrying it is the expected, standard response.

questions.q: How does SQL Server generally decide which transaction becomes the deadlock victim?
options: It generally picks the transaction that is cheapest to roll back, not necessarily the one that started the deadlock
It always picks whichever transaction started first
It always picks whichever transaction started last
It picks randomly with no consideration of rollback cost
questions.explain: The victim is typically chosen based on the cost of undoing its work, so either session involved can end up as the one killed.
